lessonTitle: Healthcare-Associated Infection: Device, Surgical-Site and Ventilator-Associated Infection

blocks.text: An 82-year-old woman admitted with a hip fracture still has a urinary catheter on day nine, placed 'for convenience' on admission. She now has a fever and confusion, and the urine grows a Gram-negative bacillus. Nothing exotic happened: a tube bridged the outside world and the bladder for nine days. Many hospital infections follow exactly this pattern, and a large share are preventable.

blocks.title: Healthcare-associated infection (HAI)
blocks.text: An infection that was not present or incubating at admission and is acquired during or as a result of receiving healthcare, typically appearing 48 hours or more after admission. HAIs also include infections that appear after discharge but are linked to a procedure or stay.

blocks.markdown: Patients in hospital are vulnerable because they are ill, may have impaired defences, and undergo procedures that breach natural barriers (skin, mucosa, airway, urinary tract). Hospital flora are often more antibiotic-resistant than community flora, which makes treatment harder. The main types are tabulated below.

blocks.caption: Main types of healthcare-associated infection
rows: Catheter-associated urinary tract infection (CAUTI)
Urinary infection in a patient with a urinary catheter; bacteria ascend along or within the catheter
E. coli, Klebsiella, Proteus, Pseudomonas, Enterococcus, Candida
Central line-associated bloodstream infection (CLABSI)
Bloodstream infection linked to a central venous catheter; skin organisms migrate along the line or hub contamination
Coagulase-negative staphylococci, S. aureus, Gram-negative bacilli, Candida
Surgical site infection (SSI)
Infection of the incision, deeper tissues or organ space within about 30 days of surgery (up to 90 days with an implant)
S. aureus, coagulase-negative staphylococci, enteric bacilli, enterococci
Ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP)
Pneumonia arising 48 hours or more after endotracheal intubation; aspiration of colonised secretions around the tube
Pseudomonas aeruginosa, S. aureus, Klebsiella, Acinetobacter
Clostridioides difficile infection
Antibiotic-associated colitis spread by spores
C. difficile

blocks.markdown: **Why devices cause persistent infection: biofilm.** A foreign body is rapidly coated by host proteins (a conditioning film). Bacteria attach, multiply, and secrete an **extracellular polymeric matrix** of polysaccharide, protein and extracellular DNA, forming a **biofilm**. Within it bacteria are in a protected community: they grow slowly and many are dormant "**persister**" cells; the matrix impedes penetration of antibiotics and antibody and shields bacteria from phagocytes; and bacteria exchange resistance genes at high density. Biofilm bacteria can tolerate antibiotic concentrations far above those that kill free-floating (planktonic) cells. Pieces and individual cells **detach** and seed the bloodstream or urine, so symptoms recur whenever antibiotics are stopped. Because the biofilm sits on the device, the infection usually cannot be cured with the device in place: **removal or replacement of the catheter or line** is a key part of treatment.

blocks.title: Why antibiotics alone fail on a colonised line
blocks.prompt: A patient with a central venous catheter has repeated positive blood cultures with coagulase-negative staphylococci. Fever resolves on antibiotics but returns after the course. Explain.

steps.text: Coagulase-negative staphylococci are skin organisms that attach to plastic and form biofilm on the catheter.
In the biofilm, bacteria are slow-growing, shielded by the matrix and tolerant of antibiotics, so planktonic cells are killed but the biofilm survives.
When antibiotics stop, shed biofilm cells reseed the bloodstream and fever recurs. The source must be removed.

blocks.answer: A biofilm on the catheter is the persistent source; removing the line is usually needed as well as antibiotics.

blocks.markdown: **Preventing catheter-associated urinary tract infection (CAUTI).** The risk rises with each day a catheter remains in place, so the most effective measure is **not inserting a catheter unless clearly indicated** and **removing it as soon as it is no longer needed**, with a daily review of need. Other measures: use **aseptic technique** and hand hygiene for insertion and handling; keep a **closed drainage system** (do not disconnect the bag); keep the bag **below bladder level** and off the floor; keep the catheter secured and use the smallest suitable size; empty the bag using clean technique; and consider alternatives such as intermittent catheterisation. Do **not** give routine antibiotics to prevent infection, do not routinely irrigate the bladder, and do not treat asymptomatic bacteriuria.

blocks.title: Calculating a device-associated rate
blocks.prompt: A unit records 6 CAUTIs over 2 400 catheter-days. Calculate the CAUTI rate per 1000 catheter-days.

blocks.caption: Prevention bundles by infection type
rows: CAUTI
Avoid unnecessary catheters, remove early, aseptic insertion, closed drainage, daily review
CLABSI
Hand hygiene, full barrier precautions and skin antisepsis at insertion, review need daily, aseptic hub handling
SSI
Appropriate timing of antibiotic prophylaxis when indicated, skin antisepsis, minimise theatre traffic, normothermia, avoid unnecessary hair removal (clip if needed)
VAP
Minimise duration of ventilation, head-of-bed elevation, oral care, subglottic secretion management, sedation holds

items: HAI is acquired through healthcare and is often device-related.
Biofilms form on catheters and lines; the matrix and slow growth protect bacteria.
Biofilm infection usually needs removal of the device.
Best CAUTI prevention: avoid and remove catheters early, aseptic technique, closed drainage.

blocks.title: Every device is a risk
blocks.text: The most effective way to prevent device-related infection is to avoid placing the device or to remove it as soon as it is not needed.

blocks.title: Do not treat a positive culture alone
blocks.text: Bacteria in the urine of a catheterised patient without symptoms usually represent colonisation, and treating it adds resistance pressure without benefit. Treat symptoms and signs of infection, not just a laboratory result.

points: HAIs include CAUTI, CLABSI, SSI, VAP and C. difficile infection.
Biofilms on devices protect bacteria from antibiotics and immunity and release cells that cause recurrent infection; removing the device is often essential.
CAUTI is reduced by avoiding catheters, early removal, aseptic technique, closed drainage and not treating asymptomatic bacteriuria.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a ventilator-associated infection?

options.text: Pneumonia developing 72 hours after endotracheal intubation
Cystitis in a patient with a urinary catheter
A wound infection after surgery
Bloodstream infection from a central line

questions.correctOptionText: Pneumonia developing 72 hours after endotracheal intubation

distractorRationale.c: That is a surgical site infection.

questions.explanation: VAP is pneumonia arising 48 hours or more after intubation, often from aspiration of colonised secretions. The other options describe different device or procedure-related infections.

questions.stem: Which organism group most commonly causes central line-associated bloodstream infection?

options.text: Coagulase-negative staphylococci and Staphylococcus aureus
Neisseria gonorrhoeae
Treponema pallidum
Plasmodium species

distractorRationale.a: Correct: skin organisms that attach to catheters.

questions.explanation: Skin flora migrate along the catheter or contaminate the hub, and staphylococci readily attach to plastic. Gram-negative bacilli and Candida are other important causes.

questions.stem: Why are biofilm-associated infections on catheters difficult to eradicate with antibiotics alone?

options.text: The matrix and slow-growing persister cells reduce antibiotic penetration and activity, and shed cells reseed infection
Biofilm bacteria are always resistant by mutation of every target
Biofilms prevent bacteria from multiplying at all
Biofilm only forms on living tissue, not on plastic

questions.correctOptionText: The matrix and slow-growing persister cells reduce antibiotic penetration and activity, and shed cells reseed infection

distractorRationale.b: Biofilm tolerance is largely physiological, not due to mutation in every cell.
distractorRationale.c: Bacteria in biofilms do grow, often slowly.
distractorRationale.d: Biofilm readily forms on plastic devices.

questions.explanation: The extracellular matrix limits drug diffusion and protects against phagocytes, and slow-growing cells are less affected by antibiotics. Cells released from the biofilm cause relapses after treatment.

questions.stem: Which measure is most effective in reducing catheter-associated urinary tract infection?

options.text: Avoiding unnecessary catheterisation and removing catheters as soon as they are not needed
Giving routine prophylactic antibiotics to all catheterised patients
Irrigating the bladder daily with antiseptic
Changing the drainage bag by disconnecting the system every day

questions.correctOptionText: Avoiding unnecessary catheterisation and removing catheters as soon as they are not needed

distractorRationale.b: Routine prophylaxis promotes resistance and is not recommended.
distractorRationale.c: Routine bladder irrigation is not recommended.
distractorRationale.d: Breaking the closed system increases risk.

questions.explanation: The risk of CAUTI increases with every day of catheterisation, so duration is the main modifiable factor. Keeping a closed drainage system and aseptic technique further reduce risk.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man with a long-term urinary catheter has a positive urine culture but no fever, dysuria, suprapubic pain or confusion. What is the appropriate approach?

options.text: Recognise asymptomatic bacteriuria, avoid antibiotics, and review whether the catheter is still needed
Start broad-spectrum antibiotics because the culture is positive
Flush the bladder with antibiotic solution
Add a prophylactic antibiotic indefinitely

questions.correctOptionText: Recognise asymptomatic bacteriuria, avoid antibiotics, and review whether the catheter is still needed

distractorRationale.b: Treating asymptomatic bacteriuria adds resistance without benefit.

questions.explanation: A catheter is nearly always colonised, so a positive culture without symptoms does not represent infection. The useful action is to ask whether the catheter can be removed.

questions.stem: A medical unit records 9 catheter-associated urinary tract infections over 4 500 catheter-days. Calculate the CAUTI rate per 1000 catheter-days.
questions.explanation: Rate = 9 / 4500 x 1000 = 2.0 per 1000 catheter-days. Using device-days as the denominator allows units with different catheter use to be compared fairly.

questions.stem: Over one quarter, a surgical ward records 15 surgical site infections in 600 operations. Calculate the surgical site infection rate as a percentage of operations.
questions.explanation: SSI rate = 15 / 600 x 100 = 2.5%. Surveillance of SSI rates, with feedback to surgeons, is a recognised way to reduce them.

questions.stem: Identify the main types of healthcare-associated infection and give one common causative organism and one preventive measure for any three of them.
markingGuide: Types: CAUTI, CLABSI, SSI, VAP, C. difficile infection
CAUTI: E. coli or other Gram-negative bacilli; avoid and remove catheters early
CLABSI: coagulase-negative staphylococci or S. aureus; aseptic insertion and daily review of need
SSI: S. aureus; skin antisepsis and appropriate antibiotic prophylaxis timing
VAP: Pseudomonas aeruginosa or S. aureus; minimise ventilation, head-of-bed elevation
questions.explanation: Each infection type has typical organisms and a prevention bundle. Answers should link the mechanism to the measure.

questions.stem: Explain how a biofilm on an intravascular catheter promotes persistent or relapsing infection, and why removing the catheter is often necessary.
markingGuide: Bacteria attach to the plastic and secrete extracellular polymeric matrix
Matrix impairs penetration of antibiotics and antibody and protects against phagocytes
Slow growth and persister cells tolerate antibiotics
Detached cells seed the bloodstream causing relapse after antibiotics stop
Eradication usually requires removal or replacement of the device
questions.explanation: The biofilm is a protected reservoir attached to the device. Without removing it, antibiotics only clear free cells.

questions.stem: List measures that reduce catheter-associated urinary tract infection and explain why routine antibiotic prophylaxis is not among them.
markingGuide: Avoid unnecessary catheterisation and use alternatives
Closed drainage system, bag below bladder level
Prophylaxis promotes resistance and does not prevent colonisation of the biofilm
questions.explanation: Duration of catheterisation is the main risk factor, so reducing it is the most effective step. Prophylaxis selects for resistant organisms without eliminating risk.
